title: Alting’s two modes of ‘deleted’ sins: decree/death vs effective application—absolute pre-faith talk is dangerous
source_text: XX. Et certe non alia mens videtur esse illorum ipsorum Theologorum, qui dicunt prius nobis peccata esse remissa, quam credamus. Nam eorum nonnulli, ut inter alios Henricus Altingius, observant peccata nostra deleta dici posse duobus modis: primo quoad decretum Dei, & mortem Christi ex decreto illo jam obitam: Secundo vero quoad efficacem applicationem, tum ex parte Christi donantis remissionem peccatorum, tum ex parte credentium fide eam accipientium. Et primo quidem modo peccata nostra deleta & remissa esse, priusquam credamus; secundo modo vero non nisi quum actu credimus, illa deleri & remitti. Sed certe hoc non sufficit, ut simpliciter & absolute dicamus peccata nobis esse remissa ante fidem. Quum enim audimus nobis remissa esse peccata, statim in mentem nobis venit remissio peccatorum non decreta solum & sub certa conditione impetrata, sed actu concessa atque applicata. Ac proinde sic loqui periculosum est, nec satis accuratum, & calumniae non parum obnoxium. * Locor. comm. part. 2. Controv. 2. de Fide Justif. contra Samosatenianos.
pass_a_gloss: And certainly the mind of those very theologians who say sins are remitted to us before we believe does not seem to be otherwise. For some of them, among others Henry Alting, observe that our sins can be said to be deleted in two ways: first with respect to God’s decree and Christ’s death already undergone from that decree; second with respect to efficacious application, both on Christ’s part giving remission of sins and on believers’ part receiving it by faith. And in the first way indeed our sins are deleted and remitted before we believe; but in the second way they are deleted and remitted only when we actually believe. But certainly this does not suffice for us to say simply and absolutely that sins are remitted to us before faith. For when we hear that sins have been remitted to us, there immediately comes into our mind remission of sins not only decreed and obtained under a certain condition, but actually granted and applied. And therefore to speak thus is dangerous, and not accurate enough, and not a little exposed to calumny. * Common Places, part 2, Controversy 2, on Justifying Faith against the Samosatenians.
pass_b_english: Alting’s two senses: decree-and-cross vs efficacious application at believing.
Absolute ‘remitted before faith’ still misleads hearers toward actual granted pardon—dangerous and calumny-prone.
